steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on ModuLoRA, a memory-efficient method for finetuning low-precision LLMs on consumer GPUs that works with arbitrary quantizers. Cover the motivation, how the method works at a high level, the main results, and a contributions summary.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- LLMs are strong but huge; need efficient finetuning
- ModuLoRA: what it is, what hardware it runs on
- How it works: low-rank adapters over quantized weights, quantizer-agnostic backward pass
- LLMTools release and results with OPTQ and QuIP#
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation
  - LLMs excel: code generation, instruction following, reasoning (cite)
  - often hundreds of billions of parameters -> hard to deploy on downstream tasks; motivates efficient finetuning (cite)
- ModuLoRA (modular low-rank adaptation)
  - memory-efficient finetuning for LLMs on consumer-grade hardware
  - 3-bit: LLaMA-30B (cite) on one Nvidia RTX 3090 24GB; LLaMA-65B on one RTX A6000 48GB
  - 2-bit: LLaMA-30B or LLaMA-65B on one RTX 3090 24GB
- Method
  - high-precision low-rank adapters on low-precision 3-bit or 4-bit weights of frozen base LLM from modern quantization algorithms (cite)
  - no own quantization procedure; integrates with user-defined quantizers via simple quantization-agnostic backward pass
  - backward pass adaptively materializes low-precision weights from black-box quantizer, combines with adapters
- Release and results
  - part of LLMTools, user-friendly library for finetuning LLMs on consumer GPUs
  - with OPTQ (cite): first 3-bit finetuning, often beats less sophisticated 4-bit and 8-bit methods
  - with QuIP# (cite): first 2-bit finetuning, matches 4-bit and 8-bit methods
  - classification, natural language inference, instruction following: competitive with much less memory
  - summarization benchmark: new state-of-the-art ROUGE with quantized LLaMA-65B
  - open-source all low-precision models, incl. first 3-bit Alpaca family, multiple sizes
  - high performance possible with smaller quantized LLMs than thought
- Contributions
  - (1) ModuLoRA over low-precision weights from user-specified black-box quantizer
  - (2) LLMTools Python library, implementation of ModuLoRA, finetune largest LLMs on consumer GPUs
  - (3) empirical evidence: smaller LLM can achieve high downstream performance

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (LLMs) do very well on many different tasks like code generation, instruction following, and reasoning. But these models are massive, often with hundreds of billions of parameters, and this makes them hard to deploy on downstream tasks and motivates research into efficient finetuning algorithms.

In this paper we propose modular low-rank adaptation (ModuLoRA), which is a memory-efficient finetuning algorithm for large language models (LLMs) that runs on consumer-grade hardware. For example, in 3-bit precision ModuLoRA can finetune a LLaMA-30B model on one Nvidia RTX 3090 24GB GPU, and a LLaMA-65B on one RTX A6000 48GB GPU. In 2-bit precision, ModuLoRA can finetune a LLaMA-30B or LLaMA-65B on one Nvidia RTX 3090 24GB GPU.

Our approach adds high-precision low-rank adapters to the low-precision 3-bit or 4-bit weights of a frozen base LLM, which are obtained with modern quantization algorithms. The important thing is that ModuLoRA does not specify its own quantization procedure. Instead it integrates with user-defined quantizers through a simple backward pass that is quantization-agnostic. This backward pass adaptively materializes the low-precision LLM weights that come from a black-box quantizer and integrates them with the high-precision low-rank adapters.

- Release: ModuLoRA in LLMTools (user-friendly library, finetuning LLMs on consumer GPUs)
  - + OPTQ: first 3-bit finetuning, often better than less sophisticated 4-bit and 8-bit quantization methods
  - + QuIP#: first 2-bit finetuning, matches 4-bit and 8-bit methods
  - classification, NLI, instruction following: competitive, much less memory
  - summarization: new state-of-the-art ROUGE with quantized LLaMA-65B
  - open-source all low-precision models, first 3-bit Alpaca family at multiple sizes
  - smaller quantized LLMs can perform well
- Contributions: (1) ModuLoRA with black-box quantization module; (2) LLMTools library; (3) evidence that a smaller LLM is enough for high downstream performance

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (LLMs) do very well on many different tasks like code generation, instruction following, and reasoning. But these models are massive, often with hundreds of billions of parameters, and this makes them hard to deploy on downstream tasks and motivates research into efficient finetuning algorithms.

In this paper we propose modular low-rank adaptation (ModuLoRA), which is a memory-efficient finetuning algorithm for large language models (LLMs) that runs on consumer-grade hardware. For example, in 3-bit precision ModuLoRA can finetune a LLaMA-30B model on one Nvidia RTX 3090 24GB GPU, and a LLaMA-65B on one RTX A6000 48GB GPU. In 2-bit precision, ModuLoRA can finetune a LLaMA-30B or LLaMA-65B on one Nvidia RTX 3090 24GB GPU.

Our approach adds high-precision low-rank adapters to the low-precision 3-bit or 4-bit weights of a frozen base LLM, which are obtained with modern quantization algorithms. The important thing is that ModuLoRA does not specify its own quantization procedure. Instead it integrates with user-defined quantizers through a simple backward pass that is quantization-agnostic. This backward pass adaptively materializes the low-precision LLM weights that come from a black-box quantizer and integrates them with the high-precision low-rank adapters.

We release ModuLoRA as part of LLMTools, which is a user-friendly library for finetuning LLMs on consumer GPUs. With the modern OPTQ quantizer, ModuLoRA makes it possible to finetune 3-bit LLMs for the first time, and it often does better than methods based on less sophisticated 4-bit and 8-bit quantization. With the state-of-the-art QuIP# quantizer, ModuLoRA makes it possible to finetune 2-bit LLMs for the first time, and it matches the performance of methods on less sophisticated 4-bit and 8-bit quantization. On tasks in classification, natural language inference, and instruction following, our low-precision models get competitive performance while using a lot less memory than existing approaches. On a popular summarization benchmark we get a new state-of-the-art ROUGE score with a quantized LLaMA-65B model. We open-source all of our low-precision models, and this includes the first 3-bit family of Alpaca models, which have strong instruction-following performance at multiple model sizes. What we find is that high performance can be achieved with smaller quantized LLMs than people thought before.

Contributions. To summarize, the contributions of this paper are: (1) we propose ModuLoRA, a memory-efficient finetuning method that works over low-precision weights that come from a black-box quantization module specified by the user; (2) we release LLMTools, a user-friendly Python library that has an implementation of ModuLoRA and lets users easily finetune the largest LLMs on consumer GPUs; (3) we give empirical evidence that high performance on downstream tasks can be achieved with a smaller LLM than previously thought.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (LLMs) excel across diverse tasks such as code generation, instruction following, and reasoning [1,2,3]. However, the massive size of these models, often reaching hundreds of billions of parameters, makes them challenging to deploy on downstream tasks and motivates research into efficient finetuning algorithms [4,5].

Here, we propose modular low-rank adaptation (ModuLoRA), a memory-efficient finetuning algorithm for large language models (LLMs) that runs on consumer-grade hardware. For example, in 3-bit precision, ModuLoRA finetunes a LLaMA-30B model [6] on one Nvidia RTX 3090 24GB GPU and a LLaMA-65B on one RTX A6000 48GB GPU. In 2-bit precision, ModuLoRA finetunes a LLaMA-30B or LLaMA-65B on one Nvidia RTX 3090 24GB GPU.

Our approach adds high-precision low-rank adapters to the low-precision 3-bit or 4-bit weights of a frozen base LLM obtained via modern quantization algorithms [7,8,9]. Crucially, ModuLoRA does not specify its own quantization procedure; instead, it integrates with user-defined quantizers through a simple quantization-agnostic backward pass. This backward pass adaptively materializes low-precision LLM weights obtained from a black-box quantizer and integrates them with high-precision low-rank adapters.

We release ModuLoRA as part of LLMTools, a user-friendly library that enables finetuning LLMs on consumer GPUs. Paired with the modern OPTQ quantizer [9], ModuLoRA enables finetuning 3-bit LLMs for the first time, often outperforming methods based on less sophisticated 4-bit and 8-bit quantization. Paired with the state-of-the-art QuIP# quantizer [10,11], ModuLoRA enables finetuning 2-bit LLMs for the first time, matching the performance of methods based on less sophisticated 4-bit and 8-bit quantization. Across tasks in classification, natural language inference, and instruction following, our low-precision models achieve competitive performance while using significantly less memory than existing approaches. On a popular summarization benchmark, we attain a new state-of-the-art ROUGE score with a quantized LLaMA-65B model. We open-source all our low-precision models, including the first 3-bit family of Alpaca models, which feature strong instruction-following performance at multiple model sizes. Our findings show that high performance can be achieved with smaller quantized LLMs than previously thought.

Contributions. In summary, this paper makes the following contributions: (1) we propose ModuLoRA, a memory-efficient finetuning method that operates over low-precision weights obtained via a user-specified black-box quantization module; (2) we release LLMTools, a user-friendly Python library that implements ModuLoRA and enables users to easily finetune the largest LLMs on consumer GPUs; (3) we provide empirical evidence that high performance on downstream tasks can be achieved with a smaller LLM than previously thought.
